meaning: He who goes forth shining; the Nahuatl sun god

phonemes.desc: Unaspirated [t] with long close-mid [oː] — the macron marks a doubled vowel, two full beats, as in toː.
Alveolar [n] between open [a] vowels; a light middle syllable.
Voiceless [t], high [i], and final [w] (written uh) — the directional ending '-going, -forth' that makes the name a participle of motion.

pronunciation.approximation: 'toh-NAH-tiw' — stretch the first o for two beats; end with a quick 'tiw,' the lips rounding shut at the close.

kin.label: Nahuatl
kin.form: Tōnatiuh < tōna 'to be hot, to shine, to burn by day' + -tiuh 'one who goes' — 'he who goes forth shining' (Karttunen, Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl; Lockhart, Nahuatl as Written)

kin.label: Word-kin
kin.form: tōnalli, 'day, day-sign, solar heat' — the day of the 260-day count that every person carries as part of the soul

kin.label: Calendar kin
kin.form: He rules the trecena 13-Olin, 'Thirteen-Movement'; ollin, the earthquake sign, is his own day

pronunciation.note: Tōnatiuh is Tier 1: the macron of ō preserves the long vowel that Classical Nahuatl actually pronounced, a phonemic length the ASCII form tonatiuh erases entirely.

domains.title: Sun
domains.subtitle: Sun, Heat, Fifth Age
domains.lead: Tōnatiuh is the Nahuatl sun god of the present age — Nahui Ollin, '4-Movement,' the Fifth Sun. His name, from tōna, 'to be hot, to shine,' names the burning disk that rises only because the gods fed it their own hearts. He is the engine of the Aztec cosmos: war, tribute, and sacrifice all answer his appetite.

cards.name: Sun
cards.desc: The Fifth Sun of the present age, Nahui Ollin — '4-Movement' — who crosses the sky only while fed with hearts.

cards.name: The Shining One
cards.desc: From tōna 'to shine, to be hot' + -tiuh 'one who goes': the name itself means 'he who goes forth shining.'

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The macron of Tōnatiuh restores the long ō Classical Nahuatl actually pronounced; plain ASCII flattens the vowel to a single beat.

cards.name: Attestation
cards.desc: Painted in the Aztec codices with a frontal solar face; in Roman letters in Sahagún's Florentine Codex and the Anales de Cuauhtitlan.

symbols.name: Sun disk with face and tongue
symbols.meaning: The frontal solar face of the codices, often shown with a protruding tongue — the sacrificial blade set in the god's own mouth

symbols.name: Ollin (movement) glyph
symbols.meaning: The trembling, striped sign of earthquake and motion that names the present age — the day-sign of the Fifth Sun

symbols.name: Obsidian knife (itztli)
symbols.meaning: The blade with which Quetzalcoatl opened the gods' breasts to feed the unmoving sun

symbols.name: Eagle (cuāuhtli)
symbols.meaning: The warrior-bird whose spirits — the eagle and jaguar dead — take up the sun's burden from noon onward

symbols.name: Sacrificial blood
symbols.meaning: The nourishment without which the sun stands still; the cosmic debt paid at every temple

mythology.lead: Tōnatiuh's mythology is the mythology of the Fifth Sun — the age we inhabit. The Nahuatl sources preserve the legend of how our sky was lit, and together they make daylight a running debt: the sun was born of a god's courage at Teotihuacan, and it moves only while it is fed.

myths.title: Nahui Ollin — The Sun of Movement
myths.text: Before our sky there were four suns, each destroyed: 4-Jaguar, when jaguars devoured the giants; 4-Wind, when hurricanes swept the people from the earth; 4-Rain of Fire, when the sky rained flames; 4-Water, when the flood came and the people became fish (Anales de Cuauhtitlan; Codex Vaticanus A). After the flood the gods gathered in darkness at Teotihuacan, the 'Place Where the Gods Were Made,' and asked who would light the world. The proud Tecuciztecatl and the humble, pox-scabbed god Nanahuatzin both offered to leap into the great fire. Tecuciztecatl faltered at the flames and leapt only at the shaming of the others; Nanahuatzin, who had no pride to lose, plunged straight in — and rose as the new sun, the moon following ashamed behind him (Florentine Codex, Book VII). Our age is therefore Nahui Ollin, '4-Movement,' and its sign is the earthquake: the sun of the present world moves, and everything that moves can end. The old gods did not make our sky to last — they made it to be paid for.

myths.title: The Sun That Demands Hearts
myths.text: When the new sun rose it would not move. 'How shall I live?' it said. 'I cannot move — feed me, nourish me' (Anales de Cuauhtitlan). The gods understood at once: no sun moves on its own strength. Quetzalcoatl took the obsidian blade, and the gods went willingly to be opened — their hearts fed the fire, and only then did the sun begin its road across the sky. The chronicles and codices name this sun Tōnatiuh, 'he who goes forth shining,' the same deity the fate-books enthrone at 13-Olin in the tonalamatl (Codex Borbonicus; Codex Vaticanus A). The tellings differ on the fire-leaper's name — Nanahuatzin in Sahagún's version, Tōnatiuh in the calendar books — but they agree completely on the economy: daylight is a loan, and the debt is paid in what is most alive. Aztec war, tribute, and temple sacrifice are not cruelty for its own sake in this theology; they are the interest on the world's first meal.

myths.title: Carried by the Warrior Dead
myths.text: All day Tōnatiuh must be carried. From dawn to noon he climbs on his own heat; at noon his strength wavers, and the souls of warriors who died in battle and of those taken by the water take up the burden — the eagle-warriors lifting him on their wings toward the west (Florentine Codex, Books II and VII). Below, his light is warred over by the tzitzimime, the star-demons who wait at the edges of the sky for the world to end; when the sun darkens in eclipse they descend to devour humanity, and the people raise a din of war-cries and drumbeats to drive them back. At evening Tōnatiuh sinks into the west and the dead warriors set him down, their service done until tomorrow's climb (Florentine Codex, Book VII). The myth makes the noon sky a battlefield: every noon is a held bridge, every dusk a narrow escape, and every eclipse the world's enemies testing the door. A sun that must be carried is a sun that can be dropped — and the whole apparatus of Aztec war exists, in this theology, to keep the bearers numerous and willing.

myths.title: 13-Olin and the Day of the Sun
myths.text: In the 260-day tonalpohualli, Tōnatiuh rules the trecena 13-Olin, 'Thirteen-Movement,' and his own day-sign is ollin — the 'earthquake, movement' glyph, drawn as a striped sign of trembling whose center carries heart-shapes. The Codex Borbonicus enthrones him inside the day-sign 4-Ollin, the very sign that names our world-age, with the emblems of the four past suns arrayed around him; the Codex Vaticanus A shows the sun's face flanked by the signs of the destroyed ages. The tonalamatl, the book of days, read a person's fate from the day-sign that ruled at birth — from 13-Olin came rulers and speakers, but also lives marked by the earthquake's instability (Sahagún, Florentine Codex, Book IV). The calendar thus makes time itself the god's body: every day is a station of his road, every thirteen-day count a circuit of his house, and every human destiny a position measured against his movement. To be born under a day of the sun was to owe the sun a life.

lore.syncretism: In the colonial centuries Tōnatiuh was mapped onto Christ — the rising sun read as the risen Son, an equation early missionaries exploited from both sides and Nahua communities adapted, so that reverence for the dawn survived inside Christian liturgy (Durán, Book of the Gods; Ricard, The Spiritual Conquest of Mexico). The old calendar lived on under saints' days while the tonalpohualli was driven into the villages. In the twentieth century the figure returned as a national one: the so-called Aztec Sun Stone, excavated in 1790, became the emblem of Mexico, its central frontal face usually identified as Tōnatiuh — though some scholars read the earth-monster or the night-lord there instead. Unlike the Greek Helios, who dissolved into allegory, Tōnatiuh never stopped being worshipped; he changed altars, and then changed back.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Piedra del Sol — the Aztec Sun Stone excavated beside Mexico City's cathedral in 1790 — hangs in the National Museum of Anthropology as the single most reproduced image of ancient Mexico, its solar face on coins, textbooks, and murals. The muralists of the revolutionary decades, Diego Rivera foremost, drew the Aztec cosmos as the deep past of the modern nation, and the sun's face entered the vocabulary of twentieth-century art. The name Tōnatiuh has returned as a given name in Mexico and in Nahuatl-language revitalization; it names schools, cultural groups, and festivals — a deity's rebirth as civic memory, and proof that a language's oldest word for the sun still knows how to shine in new mouths.
lore.extendedMeditation: Other traditions gave the sun a chariot and a serene arc; the Nahuatl tradition gave it an appetite. Tōnatiuh is the rare sun-god whose defining trait is need — he is the engine of the world and the world's greatest debtor, and every human institution of the Aztec state answers to his hunger. There is a terrible clarity in this theology: the universe is not maintained by goodwill but by payment, and the most precious coin is life itself. The legend does not flatter the payer and does not apologize for the price; it simply refuses the illusion that anything shines for free. To meditate on Tōnatiuh is to ask what keeps one's own sky moving — what daily sacrifice, great or small, feeds the light we live by.
lore.archaeology: The Great Temple (Templo Mayor) of Tenochtitlan, excavated from 1978 onward, was the engine-house of the sun cult: its building phases and offering caches — including the great Tlaltecuhtli earth-monolith and sacrificed warriors — anchor the theology in material practice. The Piedra del Sol, found in 1790 and now the centerpiece of the Museo Nacional de Antropología, bears the frontal face usually identified as Tōnatiuh (though the earth-monster and the night-lord have their defenders). The Codex Borbonicus (Bibliothèque de l'Assemblée nationale, Paris) shows his enthronement in the trecena 13-Olin. Teotihuacan — the pyramids named in the legend as the sun's birthplace — preserves an older, different solar cult a thousand years before the Aztecs, and its Pyramid of the Sun shows how deep the nameless reverence for this site ran.
